subtopic_detail: student with cramping on the first two days of each period since her cycles became regular
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old girl who has cramping lower abdominal pain on the first two days of every period. It began about eighteen months after her first period, which was at twelve, and has been present with every cycle since. She describes it as coming in waves low down in the middle, sometimes with an ache into her thighs and some loose bowel motions on the first day.

She has missed three days of school this term. Her cycles are regular at 29 days with four days of bleeding that soaks four pads a day, and there is no bleeding between periods. She is not sexually active. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g as needed on the worst day with partial benefit, starting once the pain is established. Abdominal examination is soft with no masses or tenderness today, and she is systemically well with no weight loss and no urinary or bowel symptoms between periods.

data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, no palpable mass, normal secondary sexual characteristics
data_table.Menstrual history: Menarche at twelve, regular 29 day cycles, four days of bleeding, four pads per day, no intermenstrual bleeding
data_table.Current treatment: Paracetamol 1 g as required, started after pain onset, with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for a diagnostic laparoscopy to look for peritoneal deposits and adhesions
options.rationale: Laparoscopy investigates endometriosis, the near pair, which is suggested by pain extending beyond the bleeding days, deep pain with intercourse, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, or failure of medical treatment. None of those features is present and no treatment has yet been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

options.text: Refer for a transvaginal ultrasound scan of the pelvis before starting any medical treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for atypical features, an abnormal examination or treatment failure, and transvaginal scanning is inappropriate in a young woman who is not sexually active. A normal scan would not change first line management. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Commence a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug started before the pain each cycle
options.rationale: Pain beginning within two years of menarche with regular cycles and no symptoms between periods is primary dysmenorrhoea, driven by endometrial prostaglandin release. Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis is the mechanism specific treatment and works best when started before or at the onset of bleeding rather than once the pain is established. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Increase her paracetamol to 1 g four times daily throughout each day of bleeding
options.rationale: Regular rather than as needed dosing is a genuine improvement on what she is doing and is a reasonable adjunct, so this is the closest wrong answer. Paracetamol does not inhibit peripheral prostaglandin synthesis in the endometrium and is consistently less effective than a non steroidal agent for this indication. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence a monophasic combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is effective and is the usual second line, or the first choice when contraception is also wanted. It is not the initial step for an adolescent whose simple analgesia has never been optimised and who has not tried a prostaglandin inhibitor. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without identifiable pelvic pathology and affects up to three quarters of adolescents, making it a leading cause of school absence in this age group. Pain arises from prostaglandin F2 alpha released by the shedding endometrium, which causes myometrial contraction and ischaemia, and the same prostaglandins explain the accompanying nausea and diarrhoea. It characteristically begins six to twenty four months after menarche, once ovulatory cycles are established, and is confined to the first day or two of bleeding. Features that should prompt reconsideration include onset with the very first period, pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, and failure to respond to adequate medical treatment, all of which raise endometriosis or an obstructive anomaly. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, combined hormonal contraception is the usual next step, and the two can be used together.
key_points: Onset six to twenty four months after menarche with pain confined to the bleeding days.
Prostaglandin mediated, which is why non steroidal agents outperform paracetamol.
Dosing should begin before or at the onset of bleeding, not after pain is established.
Combined hormonal contraception is second line or first when contraception is wanted.
Pain outside menstruation or treatment failure should prompt evaluation for endometriosis.
explanation.pearls: Mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily, started one day before the expected period and continued for the first two to three days, is the standard Australian regimen, and taking it pre emptively rather than reactively is what converts a partial response into a complete one.

subtopic_detail: premenopausal woman with spotting between periods and a focal echogenic lesion within the cavity
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman with eight months of light spotting that occurs about a week before each period. Her periods themselves remain regular at 30 days and are not heavy, and she has no pain. She has two children, is not using hormonal contraception, and her partner has had a vasectomy.

Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, and speculum examination at that visit showed a normal cervix. She has no risk factors for endometrial cancer and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. A transvaginal ultrasound arranged at her last visit reports a well defined echogenic lesion measuring 14 mm within the endometrial cavity with a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, surrounded by normal appearing endometrium. Both ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid. A full blood examination shows haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155).

data_table.Examination: Normal cervix on speculum, mobile anteverted uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: well defined 14 mm echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel, normal surrounding endometrium and normal ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155), human papillomavirus testing negative six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an outpatient endometrial pipelle sampling in the consulting room this afternoon
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling reliably detects diffuse endometrial pathology such as hyperplasia or carcinoma, but it samples only a fraction of the cavity and frequently misses a focal lesion entirely. A negative result would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase of her next menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Timing a scan to days five to ten is the right way to reduce false positives when the endometrium looks thickened and non specific, since secretory endometrium can mimic pathology. A discrete lesion with its own feeding vessel is already a definite finding. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid during bleeding days and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy reduces menstrual blood loss but has no effect on intermenstrual spotting from a structural lesion, and her blood count is normal so volume is not the problem. This treats the wrong element of her presentation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the lesion with the specimen sent for histology
options.rationale: A well defined echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel is an endometrial polyp, and hysteroscopic resection under direct vision both cures the bleeding and provides tissue. It is the definitive investigation and treatment in one procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to control the intermenstrual spotting
options.rationale: The intrauterine system is excellent for heavy menstrual bleeding once the cavity is known to be normal, and it does thin the endometrium. Placing it over an undiagnosed focal lesion leaves the pathology in place and commonly causes further unscheduled bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Endometrial polyps are focal overgrowths of endometrial glands and stroma with a fibrovascular core, and they are a common structural cause of intermenstrual bleeding in women in their thirties and forties. On transvaginal ultrasound they appear as well defined echogenic intracavity lesions, and the single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, sometimes called the pedicle artery sign, is characteristic. The key management principle is that focal lesions need focal sampling: blind endometrial biopsy is designed for diffuse pathology and has poor sensitivity for a discrete polyp, so hysteroscopy is required. Malignancy within a polyp is uncommon in premenopausal women at well under two per cent, but rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size, so histology is always obtained. Saline infusion sonohysterography is an alternative way of delineating the cavity where hysteroscopy access is limited.
key_points: Intermenstrual bleeding with a discrete echogenic intracavity lesion suggests a polyp.
A single feeding vessel on colour Doppler supports the diagnosis.
Blind pipelle sampling has poor sensitivity for focal lesions.
Hysteroscopic resection is diagnostic and therapeutic in the same procedure.
Malignancy risk rises with age, postmenopausal status, tamoxifen use and polyp size.
explanation.pearls: Measure the endometrium on days five to ten of the cycle when a scan is being arranged for abnormal bleeding in a premenopausal woman, because a secretory phase endometrium can measure over 14 mm normally and generates unnecessary referrals.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation of abnormal vaginal bleeding

subtopic_detail: woman wanting to conceive with a diffusely enlarged tender uterus and junctional zone thickening
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 36-year-old woman referred with worsening period pain and heavy bleeding over three years. She describes a constant dragging heaviness through the whole of the last week of her cycle rather than pain confined to the bleeding days, and she now takes two days off work each month.

She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eleven months. Her cycles are regular at 27 days and she passes clots, but she has never had bleeding between periods. Examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged globular uterus about the size of a ten week pregnancy, which is tender and boggy on bimanual palpation, with no adnexal masses and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone thickening of 14 mm, and small myometrial cysts. No discrete fibroid is identified and the endometrium and ovaries appear normal.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrically enlarged globular tender uterus of about ten week size, no adnexal mass, no uterosacral nodularity
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone 14 mm, myometrial cysts, normal endometrium and ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 14 mcg/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend first?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to reduce bleeding and relieve the pain
options.rationale: The intrauterine system is the most effective medical treatment for adenomyosis and would be the right answer for a woman not seeking pregnancy. It is a contraceptive, so recommending it to a woman actively trying to conceive defeats her primary goal. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy for six months
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue and is sometimes used before surgery, but it induces a hypo oestrogenic anovulatory state and so prevents conception throughout treatment. It also carries bone density consequences over that timeframe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence iron replacement with tranexamic acid during bleeding and refer to fertility services
options.rationale: Junctional zone thickening above 12 mm with a globular tender uterus and myometrial cysts is adenomyosis, and every effective suppressive treatment for it prevents conception. In a woman with an eleven month history of trying, the plan is symptom control that preserves fertility plus timely referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any peritoneal deposits identified
options.rationale: Laparoscopy targets peritoneal endometriosis, the near pair, which produces uterosacral nodularity, a fixed retroverted uterus and deep pain with intercourse rather than a symmetrically enlarged boggy uterus. Adenomyosis lies within the myometrium and is not diagnosed or treated by looking at the peritoneum. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce both the bleeding and the uterine bulk
options.rationale: Embolisation does improve adenomyosis symptoms but risks ovarian and endometrial injury and is generally avoided in women with a current pregnancy intention. It is offered mainly to women who have completed their families. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, producing a diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heavy painful periods and a characteristic dragging pelvic heaviness. Ultrasound features include a globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, linear striations and a thickened or irregular junctional zone, with a junctional zone of 12 mm or more being widely used as a threshold. It is increasingly recognised as a contributor to subfertility and to miscarriage and preterm birth, probably through disrupted junctional zone peristalsis and impaired implantation. The central management tension is that the effective treatments, including the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonists, continuous progestogens and embolisation, are all incompatible with conceiving. For the woman trying to conceive, treatment is therefore limited to fertility sparing symptom control with iron replacement, tranexamic acid and non steroidal analgesia, alongside prompt referral for assisted reproduction where indicated.
key_points: Globular tender uterus with junctional zone thickening above 12 mm suggests adenomyosis.
Endometriosis is distinguished by uterosacral nodularity and a fixed retroverted uterus.
Most effective treatments are contraceptive and therefore unavailable when conception is the goal.
Correct iron deficiency and use tranexamic acid for bleeding while fertility is being pursued.
Adenomyosis is associated with subfertility, miscarriage and preterm birth.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g three to four times daily for the first three to four days of bleeding reduces menstrual blood loss by roughly 40 per cent without affecting ovulation or conception, which makes it the workhorse for heavy bleeding in a woman actively trying to become pregnant.

subtopic_detail: breastfeeding woman with severe shooting pain and blanching of the nipple starting after the feed ends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. She describes severe burning pain in both nipples that comes on a minute or two after the baby comes off the breast and lasts about ten minutes, and she has started dreading feeds. It is much worse when she gets out of the shower or takes the washing off the line on a cold morning.

A lactation consultant reviewed the attachment last week and was satisfied with it, and the baby has regained birth weight and is now gaining 190 g per week. She has completed a course of oral fluconazole and two weeks of topical miconazole prescribed by a colleague, with no improvement. On examination the nipples are intact with no cracks, fissures or discharge, and the areolae and breasts are soft with no erythema, lump or warmth. As you examine her, the tip of the left nipple blanches white, then becomes dusky blue, and then flushes red as the pain she describes builds. She takes no regular medications and has cold hands in winter.

data_table.Examination: Intact nipples with no fissures, cracks or discharge, soft non erythematous breasts with no palpable lump
data_table.Provoked finding: Triphasic white then blue then red colour change of the nipple tip observed on exposure to room air
data_table.Infant: Regained birth weight, gaining 190 g per week, attachment assessed as satisfactory by a lactation consultant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her back for further attachment assessment and a review for tongue tie in the infant
options.rationale: Poor attachment and restrictive tongue tie are the commonest causes of nipple pain overall and would be the first thing to address, which is why this remains tempting. Attachment has already been assessed as satisfactory and the infant is gaining well, and neither explains cold provoked colour change. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Prescribe a longer course of oral fluconazole for her with oral nystatin drops for the baby
options.rationale: Extended antifungal therapy for mother and infant is the standard approach to candidal nipple infection, the near pair, which gives a persistent burning pain that is present during as well as after feeds and is usually accompanied by shiny or flaky areolar skin or infant oral thrush. She has already failed adequate antifungal treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Advise warmth immediately after feeds and prescribe oral nifedipine for a two week trial
options.rationale: A triphasic colour change with pain beginning after the feed and provoked by cold is vasospasm of the nipple, a Raynaud phenomenon, not infection. Conservative warming plus a calcium channel blocker is the established treatment and breastfeeding can continue throughout. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Advise expressing and cup feeding for two weeks to rest the nipples and allow them to heal
options.rationale: Resting the nipples helps a mechanical or traumatic injury heal, but vasospasm is triggered by the temperature drop when the nipple is exposed to air, which expressing does not avoid. It also risks undermining supply at six weeks. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm)
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

options.text: Prescribe oral di flucloxacillin for ten days and advise her to continue feeding from both sides
options.rationale: Antistaphylococcal therapy treats mastitis or an infected nipple fissure, which produces a red tender wedge of breast with systemic symptoms or a visibly broken nipple surface. Her breasts are soft and her nipple skin is intact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Nipple vasospasm is a Raynaud phenomenon of the nipple in which arteriolar constriction follows the temperature drop as the nipple leaves the warm mouth, and it is a frequently missed cause of severe persistent nipple pain in breastfeeding women. The history that identifies it is pain that starts after rather than during the feed, is described as burning or shooting, and is reliably provoked by cold, together with an observable blanching of the nipple tip. The classic triphasic white to blue to red colour change is not always complete, and blanching alone in the right clinical context is enough. It is very commonly misdiagnosed as candidal infection, and many women arrive having already failed courses of antifungal treatment for both themselves and the infant. Underlying poor attachment and nipple trauma can trigger vasospasm, so attachment must still be assessed, but once optimised the treatment is avoidance of cold, immediate warmth after feeds, and nifedipine where conservative measures fail.
key_points: Pain starting after the feed ends and provoked by cold distinguishes vasospasm.
Blanching of the nipple tip, with or without the full triphasic change, is the sign.
It is routinely misdiagnosed and treated as candidal infection without benefit.
Optimise attachment first, since nipple trauma can trigger the vasospasm.
Nifedipine is compatible with breastfeeding and works within days when it is going to work.
explanation.pearls: Nifedipine 20 mg of the modified release preparation once daily is the usual starting dose for nipple vasospasm, with response expected within about 72 hours, and only trivial amounts pass into breast milk so the infant needs no monitoring.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association and Royal Women's Hospital: Nipple vasospasm

subtopic_detail: woman unable to tolerate penetration with involuntary tightening and a normal genital examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse. She and her partner of two years have tried many times; she describes a sensation of a wall and involuntary tightening, together with burning at the entrance, and they always stop. She has never been able to insert a tampon and had to abandon an attempted cervical screening test last year.

She is distressed and says she feels she is failing her relationship. She has no history of sexual assault, no dyspareunia beyond the entrance because penetration has never occurred, and no cyclical pelvic pain, bowel or bladder symptoms. On careful inspection with her consent, the vulva looks normal with no fissures, pallor, architectural loss or erythema, and the hymenal ring is patent. Light touch with a cotton bud at the vestibule reproduces her burning and you observe visible contraction of the perineal muscles. She declines any attempt at internal examination and you do not proceed.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no pallor, fissuring, adhesions or erythema, patent hymenal ring
data_table.Provoked finding: Cotton bud touch at the vestibule reproduces burning with visible involuntary perineal muscle contraction
data_table.History: Lifelong inability to tolerate tampon insertion, cervical screening or penetrative intercourse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend?

options.text: Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation alongside psychosexual therapy
options.rationale: Lifelong inability to tolerate penetration with involuntary pelvic floor contraction and a normal vulva is genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder, in which the muscle response and the anticipatory fear maintain each other. Combined pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

options.text: Refer for examination under anaesthesia with division of any obstructing hymenal band
options.rationale: Surgery addresses an anatomical obstruction such as a microperforate hymen or a transverse vaginal septum, the structural near pair. The hymenal ring is patent on inspection here, and operating on a normal introitus reinforces the belief that something is physically wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

options.text: Arrange injection of botulinum toxin into the levator ani muscles under conscious sedation
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is studied as a third line option for refractory cases and is not first line, since it does not address the cognitive and behavioural components. Offering it before conservative therapy exposes her to an invasive procedure with modest evidence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vaginismus)

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks and arrange a further review after that
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats the thin pale friable epithelium of genitourinary syndrome of menopause or of prolonged lactational hypo oestrogenism. A well oestrogenised vulva in a 26 year old with normal cycles will not respond to it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe topical lignocaine gel for use before intercourse and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Topical anaesthetic is a reasonable adjunct that some women use alongside desensitisation work, so it is not a wrong treatment in itself. Used alone it numbs the vestibular pain without addressing the involuntary muscle response that physically prevents penetration. (Source: RANZCOG: Female sexual dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Genito pelvic pain and penetration disorder is the current diagnostic term that unified what were previously called vaginismus and dyspareunia, and it covers difficulty with penetration, vulvovaginal pain on attempted penetration, fear of that pain, and involuntary pelvic floor tightening. Lifelong forms present exactly as this woman does, with tampons, examinations and intercourse all impossible from the outset and a structurally normal genital tract. A pain and fear cycle sustains the condition: anticipation increases pelvic floor tone, the increased tone makes penetration painful, and the pain reinforces the anticipation. Assessment must still exclude organic causes including lichen sclerosus, vulval dermatoses, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism, which is why unhurried inspection matters even when internal examination is declined. Treatment combines pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded self directed dilator work and psychosexual therapy, ideally with the partner involved, and success rates with this combination are high.
key_points: Involuntary pelvic floor contraction with a structurally normal vulva defines the disorder.
Lifelong forms prevent tampon use and clinical examination as well as intercourse.
Exclude lichen sclerosus, obstructive anomalies and hypo oestrogenism by inspection.
Pelvic floor physiotherapy plus psychosexual therapy is first line and highly effective.
Never force an internal examination; it reinforces the fear that maintains the condition.
explanation.pearls: Offering the woman control of the pace and of the instrument, including letting her place her own hand over yours or insert a dilator herself, changes outcomes measurably, because loss of control during examination is one of the strongest perpetuating factors in this disorder.
